None of this means deportations have stopped. People are still being arrested, detained, and deported. Families are still being separated. The harm is real and ongoing. But the gap between rhetoric and operational capacity is widening, not closing.

Trump attended oral arguments (apparently a first for a sitting president) but left after 81 minutes, departing 5 minutes into the opposing side's argument. It captured the administration's posture in miniature.

Only Justices Alito and Thomas appeared open to the government's position. Justice Kavanaugh suggested the Court could resolve the case simply by reaffirming Wong Kim Ark. ACLU attorney Cecillia Wang replied with one word: "Yes." The courtroom laughed.

The 14th Amendment has guaranteed birthright citizenship for 125+ years, reaffirmed in U.S. v. Wong Kim Ark (1898). The government's argument relied on what Chief Justice Roberts called "quirky" and "idiosyncratic" reasoning.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Trump v. Barbara this week on birthright citizenship. Every federal court has already struck the executive order down. Based on the arguments, SCOTUS appears likely to do the same.
The Idaho Sheriffs' Association wrote a letter opposing the bill. This shows that pushback on immigration enforcement isn't only about politics; it's about operational reality on the ground.

Even in Idaho (one of the most conservative states in the country) local sheriffs are opposing a bill that would mandate 287(g) partnerships statewide. Their objections are citing liability and operational overreach.

In Maine, new data shows 80% of those arrested in recent ICE operations had no criminal convictions or pending charges. That makes the "public safety" justification for expanded local enforcement very hard to sustain politically.

On local enforcement: the 287(g) program deputizes local police to do immigration work. In theory, it multiplies federal reach. In practice, it creates a fragmented "patchwork of overlapping and potentially conflicting authority" and that's exactly what we're seeing.

Despite reports of a 3,000-per-day arrest quota, daily arrest figures have consistently fallen short. The administration has never come close to the detention capacity needed to deliver deportation at the scale it promises.

Michigan has moved to freeze construction at a warehouse being converted into a detention center in Romulus, near Detroit. It may be the most consequential test yet of whether states can block federal detention expansion on the ground.

DHS has paused its bid to acquire nearly two dozen industrial warehouses for makeshift detention. This was a centerpiece of rapid detention expansion. Legal challenges, staff resistance, and leadership chaos all contributed to the pause.
I've argued since Day 1 that the main barriers to mass deportation are logistical, not just legal. The system runs on contracts, staffing, and local cooperation, all of which have real limits.
Trump's deportation machine is getting a reality check. The Supreme Court, red-state sheriffs, and DHS's own bureaucracy are all pushing back. Here's what's actually happening beneath the rhetoric. 🧵

EVENT ANNOUNCEMENT: "Untangling the Messy Politics of Immigration Data" - at GWU in DC, April 10 at 12PM. Registration required, in person only.
